summary: Comments on the TCP Big Window option described in RFC 1106, pointing to a problem with it. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6247.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1110 explains a flaw in a proposal to enlarge TCP's transmission window without enlarging its sequence number space. A delayed packet can arrive when its old number is in use again and be mistaken for new data; RFC 6247 later obsoleted this memo.

questions: problem with tcp big window option
why is tcp window size limited
how does tcp handle packet reordering
why can a tcp big window accept old packets
subtitle: Why TCP cannot safely enlarge its transmission window without more sequence numbers.

tldr.problem: The TCP Big Window proposal expands the window to 30 bits while leaving the sequence number space unchanged, which can make delayed old packets look current.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1110 explains that packet loss, reordering, and duplication can make a packet return after its sequence number has been reused within the enlarged window.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1110 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 6247. It concludes that the RFC 1106 approach cannot be used for general Internet traffic.

today: RFC 1110 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 6247.

sections.title: What Sequence Numbers Protect
sections.content:
TCP assigns sequence numbers to bytes so the receiver can put data in order. Acknowledgments, timeouts, and retransmissions address loss, while the sequence numbers help distinguish duplicate data. The sequence number is a 32-bit field and wraps after transmission of 2^32 bytes.

The transmission window and limits on packet lifetime help keep a reused number from being mistaken for an old byte. The window field is 16 bits in the design discussed by the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP numbers data so the receiver can restore the original order and spot duplicates. Those numbers eventually wrap around, so the window and packet lifetime matter too.

sections.title: How a Big Window Can Reuse Numbers Too Soon
sections.content:
The TCP Big Window option described in RFC 1106 expands the window specification to 30 bits but leaves the sequence number space unchanged. RFC 1110 says this means a sequence number can be reused after 4 round-trip times. The NAK option can cause retransmission after one round-trip time.

If a packet remains delayed in the network for about 5 round-trip times, it may arrive when the same sequence number is inside a later window. TCP may then accept the earlier data as new and fail to recreate the original data stream. The memo says this concern depends on packet reordering and duplication, which can occur in the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: If the window grows but the number space does not, TCP can reuse a number while an old packet is still delayed. That old packet can then be mistaken for new data.

sections.title: Why the Proposal Was Not General
sections.content:
RFC 1110 notes that RFC 1106 may describe an isolated satellite network where packets arrive in order or are lost, without arriving later out of order. Under that assumption, the problem would not occur. The memo concludes that the approach cannot be adopted for general Internet use, where packets can be delivered out of order.

Its stated design conclusion is that the window must not be increased without a corresponding increase in the sequence number space.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal might work in a network that never reorders packets. RFC 1110 says the Internet does reorder packets, so a larger window also needs a larger sequence number space.
